title: The ten-copy agent-contract replication idiom and its published span digest
content: This repo's agent-facing contracts (plugins/pipeline/agents/*.md, 9 files, plus the shared Phase 4 preamble in plugins/pipeline/commands/pipeline.md, 1 site -- 10 copies total) carry a shared idiom: a canonical rule passage stated byte-identically in all ten places, introduced by evidence.md's 'identical for every pipeline agent' heading convention. #40 found that idiom had ALREADY DRIFTED, 3 of 9 files, before this run touched it, and the drift direction was LOSS OF SPECIFIC MEASURED DETAIL under an unchanged heading -- the kind of drift a reader trusting the heading's promise would not notice. #40 shipped the property-not-implementation rule as a new byte-identical passage across all ten sites (span digest as merged at 7a052d3: 14b65c48479dfceefb780689adccfbd53656b21e; this value moves every time the block body changes and MUST NOT be trusted without re-computing it -- see the re-derivation command below) and, load-bearing for future edits to ANY of the ten sites, published the digest INSIDE the contract on a line immediately OUTSIDE the hashed span (a digest cannot cover itself), so a copy edited without updating its digest line fails a mechanical check loudly instead of shipping a stale, silently-trusted number. MECHANISM: the terminator line states its bounds EXPLICITLY -- from the '## The property, not the fix' heading to the end of THAT heading line, not to the next '## ' heading and not to end-of-file. Re-derivation command (script-file form; do not nest quotes on a command line, see the harness-defect note below): extract each of the ten spans by that exact bound, run `shasum` over each, and assert (a) exactly one distinct hash across all ten AND (b) count is 10 AND (c) the hash is not the empty-string digest (`da39a3ee5e6b4b0d3255bfef95601890afd80709`). FOUR FALSE-ALARM READINGS ARE NAMED IN THE SHIPPED TEXT ITSELF, because three separate readers produced a false alarm before the bounds and digest were published, and each one is output-indistinguishable from real drift unless you know which discriminator rules it out: (1) ANCHORING THE TERMINATOR (adding a `$`/end-of-line anchor the design does not carry) makes extraction run to end-of-file in every copy -- since the trailing content differs per file, this produces TEN DISTINCT HASHES, output-identical to genuine ten-way drift; the discriminator is the digest match, not the group count. (2) STOPPING AT THE NEXT '## ' HEADING instead of the terminator's own end-of-line produces a HANDFUL OF GROUPS (files whose next heading differs group differently), also readable as partial drift. (3) READING TO END OF FILE (the general case of (1) when no anchor exists to notice) is the failure mode a naive extractor falls into by default; same ten-distinct-hashes signature. (4) TRIMMING THE SPAN'S TRAILING NEWLINE is the SUBTLEST of the four and the one #40's own reviewer (QA, Phase 4) found the other three false alarms did not cover: it gives a UNIFORM hash across all ten files -- so a naive 'do all ten agree?' check PASSES -- but that hash disagrees with the published digest (measured: with the terminator line's newline, the span hashes to 3f92ab1a58e985bd1708f9d340ce08921351f42c at that round's block text; trimmed, the same three files hash to 5abd3aa40baec08c67a39d3e5eb0af310ef9e8f5, later re-confirmed at a different block revision as 0cb16ae3bdb7bf634c0daedd5fa9a3a78765257a vs the shipped 14b65c48...). This is WHY the assertion compares the DIGEST, not merely the group count: 'ten agreeing hashes that are not the published one' means the trailing newline was trimmed, not that the block is safe. A FIFTH failure mode, recorded separately because it is a harness defect rather than a reading of the bounds: #40's own implementer's first census run printed ten DISTINCT hashes on a genuinely clean tree while the battery's own equivalent cell passed, and the cause was an unexamined shell-quoting layer (a `$` anchor added to the terminator regex in a nested-quote command line that neither the design nor the extraction function carried) -- re-run from a script FILE rather than nested shell quotes, it agreed with the battery. Recorded as the general rule about proving the mutation you applied is the mutation you meant, turned on your own harness: an unexamined quoting layer can manufacture catastrophic-looking drift that isn't there. GOVERNANCE LIMIT, STATED IN THE SHIPPED TEXT ITSELF: the rule this idiom guards is stated in FOUR places and hashed in only ONE. Beyond the ten block copies, review.schema.json's remediation description and secops.md's Style bullet and VETO reply template each restate the same rule outside the hashed span, and #40's QA panel proved BOTH of those two secops.md statements mutable (reworded) without reddening the digest or any other mechanical check -- they are re-read by hand or not at all. A coherent all-ten edit (every copy changed the same way, digest and canonical text updated together in one commit) defeats census, digest and byte-identity verbatim checks TOGETHER; the one control QA found that survives it is a role-claim-vs-observed-behaviour matrix (AC4.matrix in #40's verify-40.sh) that checks each agent's stated licence against what the shipped hook actually enforces for that role, for the nine agent roles -- it does NOT cover the orchestrator's own claim, which is checked by a single substring match ('no SubagentStop at all'). A future editor of any of the ten sites must re-run the digest AND re-apply the two secops.md worked cases by hand; the mechanical check alone is not sufficient evidence of correctness.
